Lucía asks Ana to tell her how she met Mihai. Ana remembers the first day (chapter 1!).
Ana, you’ve never told me how you met Mihai.
Well… it was a Saturday in September. It was sunny and I was in the café in the square.
I was reading a book and drinking a coffee. There were lots of people.
Then a tall guy came in with a guidebook to Madrid. He looked a bit lost.
There were no free tables, so he asked me: “Can I sit here?”
How romantic! And what did you say?
I said yes. His Spanish was very bad, but he was really nice.
While we were talking, suddenly his coffee spilled all over my book.
No! And what did you do?
I laughed a lot. He went as red as a tomato and apologised ten times.
The next day he bought me a new book. That’s how it all began.
And when did you fall in love?
That’s another story… but I think it was in Romania, in the snow!

In “reí”, “reír”, “sonreír” the stress falls on the í: re-Í, son-re-ÍR.
R at the beginning of a word is rolled: rojo, romántico, repente.
1. The setting and the action: the film method
When you tell a story, you use both past tenses. Imagine you’re filming:
What the weather was like: Hacía sol.
Where I was, what I was doing: Leía un libro.
What someone did: Me preguntó algo.
The time, age: Eran las cinco. Tenía 25 años.
Precise moments: A las cinco llegó.
The magic question: “And then what happened?” If the verb answers it, it’s INDEFINIDO. If it only describes the situation, it’s IMPERFECTO.
English does something similar! “I was reading (imperfect) when he came in (indefinido).” Use your instinct: “was …ing” and “used to” usually point to the imperfect.
An action was in progress (imperfect) when something happened (indefinido):
I was reading when Mihai came in.
I was sleeping when the phone rang.
When I arrived, they were having dinner.
Don’t swap them: “Leí cuando entraba Mihai” completely changes the meaning (I read while he kept coming in…) and sounds odd.
un día, una vez (one day, once)
While we were talking, suddenly the coffee fell.
Spanish uses the plural reflexive pronouns for actions people do to each other, where English says “each other” (or nothing):
Other reciprocal verbs: enamorarse (to fall in love), casarse (to get married), besarse (to kiss), escribirse (to write to each other).
“Enamorarse DE alguien” = to fall in love WITH someone: Se enamoró de Mihai.
5. The structure of a good story
A classic story in Spanish has three parts:
Era un sábado. Hacía sol. Yo leía…

Mihai tells about a night shift in the hospital’s emergency department.
It was a Tuesday in February. It was three in the morning and it was pouring with rain.
I was on call in A&E. Everything was quiet and I was having a coffee.
Suddenly the door opened and a very agitated man came in.
He was carrying his wife in his arms. She was pregnant and in a lot of pain.
I called the gynaecologist, but she was in another operation.
There was no time. So I did it myself, with the help of a nurse.
Fifteen minutes later a beautiful baby girl was born. She weighed three kilos.
The father was crying with joy. The mother was tired, but very happy.
Then the mother asked me: “What’s your name, doctor?”
I told her: “Mihai.” She smiled and said: “Then the little girl will be called Mihaela.”
It was the most beautiful night of my career.

El gato que llegó con la lluvia
It was a November night. It was raining non-stop and a strong wind was blowing.
Lena was in her flat in Malasaña. She was reading a novel on the sofa and drinking a hot tea.
Suddenly she heard a noise on the terrace. At first she thought it was the wind.
But the noise went on: it was a faint, sad sound, like crying.
Lena opened the terrace door. There, under a plant, was a small black cat.
It was soaking wet and shaking with cold. It had very big green eyes.
Lena picked it up carefully and carried it inside. She dried it with a towel and gave it a little milk.
The cat drank it all and then fell asleep on her book.
The next day Lena asked all the neighbours, but nobody knew the cat.
She put up posters in the streets of the neighbourhood: “Is this your cat? Call this number.”
She waited a week. Nobody called.
While she was waiting, the cat started sleeping on her bed, playing with her guitar and waiting for her at the door when she came home from work.
Lena had never had a pet, because her father was allergic.
One Sunday, Tom came to visit. He saw the cat on the sofa and asked: “What’s its name?”.
Lena thought for a moment. Outside, it was starting to rain again.
“Her name is Lluvia (Rain),” she said. “She came with the rain… and she’s staying for ever.”
Since then, whenever it rains, Lluvia sits at the window and watches the drops for hours.
Lena says she’s remembering the night she found her home. Tom says she’s just waiting for dinner.
And Lena always takes Lluvia’s side.

Rosario tells how she met Grandpa Antonio.
It was the summer of 1962. I was seventeen.
There was a party in my village and everyone was dancing in the square.
I was with my friends when a dark-haired boy asked me to dance.
He danced terribly, but he had a wonderful smile.
We got married two years later. And we were together for fifty years!
